title: Linear Optimization II: Sensitivity, Duality & What-If Thinking
subtitle: The solution is the beginning, not the end — shadow prices, reduced costs, and the economics hiding inside every solved LP

objectives.title: Price your scarce resources with shadow prices
objectives.description: Answer the question every operations leader asks — 'what would I pay for one more machine-hour?' — directly from solver output.

objectives.title: Interpret reduced costs and ranging reports
objectives.description: Use reduced costs to judge why a product is out of the plan, and RHS/objective ranging to know exactly how far the numbers can drift before the answer changes.

objectives.title: Explain duality in managerial language
objectives.description: See every LP's mirror image: allocating resources versus pricing them, and why the two problems always agree at the optimum.

objectives.title: Verify models you didn't build
objectives.description: In a world where AI drafts your optimization models in seconds, use sensitivity analysis as the human sanity check that catches wrong units, absurd valuations, and broken constraints.

agenda.title: Opening Hook: The Overtime Offer
agenda.description: Your furniture shop from last week is back, and a supplier offers overtime carpentry hours at $15 each. Take the deal? Everyone votes before we solve. Then we reveal that the LP already computed the answer — the shadow price — the moment it solved. Plus: Homework #1 debrief on the blending problem.
bulletPoints: A solved LP contains a full economic report card, not just a plan
Shadow price = the objective's gain from one more unit of a resource
Homework #1 debrief: the blending formulations that worked and the ratio traps that didn't

agenda.title: Shadow Prices: The Economics of Scarcity
agenda.description: The marginal value of every constraint, computed for free. We work through binding constraints with positive shadow prices, slack constraints worth exactly zero, and the golden rule: pay less than the shadow price, profit; pay more, walk away.
bulletPoints: Binding constraint → positive shadow price; slack constraint → zero
Shadow prices are marginal — valid only within the RHS range
Refineries and airlines negotiate real contracts off these numbers daily

agenda.title: Reduced Costs & Ranging: How Far Can the Numbers Drift?
agenda.description: Why is a product at zero in the optimal plan, and what would its margin need to be to earn its way in? That's the reduced cost. Then objective and RHS ranging: the intervals within which your answer — or your shadow prices — stay valid.
bulletPoints: Reduced cost = the margin improvement needed before a zero-valued variable enters the plan
Objective ranging: how much can a price move before the plan changes?
RHS ranging: the window where each shadow price still holds

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Ten minutes to recharge before we open the hood on the dual problem.

agenda.title: Duality for Managers
agenda.description: Every LP has a twin. The primal allocates resources to maximize profit; the dual prices those resources to minimize their total valuation — and at the optimum the two objectives are equal. No theorem-proving: we build the dual of the production-mix problem and discover the dual variables are the shadow prices we already met.
bulletPoints: Primal: 'what should we make?' Dual: 'what are our resources worth?'
Strong duality: optimal profit equals the optimal valuation of resources
The dual is how economists, auctioneers, and transfer-pricing teams think

agenda.title: Hands-On Lab: Pi, RC, and Managerial What-Ifs
agenda.description: Colab time. We solve an expanded production model, pull Pi (shadow prices), RC (reduced costs), and the ranging attributes from gurobipy, and race through a rapid-fire round of what-if questions — answering each from the sensitivity report without re-solving.
bulletPoints: Answer five manager questions using only the sensitivity report
Then re-solve to verify — and find the one question ranging can't answer

agenda.title: Why AI Makes This Skill More Valuable, Not Less
agenda.description: LLMs can now draft a gurobipy model from a paragraph in seconds — which means wrong models get built faster than ever. Sensitivity analysis is your lie detector: a shadow price of $4,000 per labor-hour or a maxed-out resource valued at zero screams 'check the formulation.' Homework #2 briefing.
bulletPoints: AI generates models; humans must still certify them
Absurd shadow prices are the fastest way to catch unit errors and bad constraints
Homework #2: a sensitivity memo to a fictional COO — analytics in executive English

activities.title: The Sensitivity Interrogation
activities.description: Solve the expanded three-product furniture model, extract the full sensitivity report from gurobipy, and answer a rapid-fire set of managerial what-ifs — without re-solving the model.

steps.title: Solve and extract the report
steps.description: Run the model, then loop over constraints for Pi and slack, and over variables for RC and objective ranging. Print it as a clean table.

steps.title: Answer the what-ifs
steps.description: Overtime carpentry at $15/hour — buy it? A bookshelf line with $40 margin sits at zero — what margin would flip it in? Desk profit drops 10% — does the plan change?

steps.title: Verify by re-solving
steps.description: Change the data, re-solve, and confirm the sensitivity report predicted every outcome — until you push a RHS past its ranging limit and watch the prediction break.

steps.title: Audit an AI-drafted model
steps.description: Inspect a provided LLM-generated model whose sensitivity report contains one absurd number. Find it, diagnose the formulation bug behind it, and fix it.

codeBlock.code:
import gurobipy as gp
from gurobipy import GRB

m = gp.Model("furniture_expanded")
desks = m.addVar(name="desks")
chairs = m.addVar(name="chairs")
shelves = m.addVar(name="shelves")

m.setObjective(70*desks + 50*chairs + 40*shelves, GRB.MAXIMIZE)
m.addConstr(4*desks + 3*chairs + 2*shelves <= 240, "carpentry")
m.addConstr(2*desks + 1*chairs + 1*shelves <= 100, "finishing")
m.optimize()

print("--- Shadow prices (Pi) ---")
for c in m.getConstrs():
    print(f"{c.ConstrName}: ${c.Pi:.2f}/hour  "
          f"(valid RHS range {c.SARHSLow:.0f}-{c.SARHSUp:.0f})")

print("--- Reduced costs (RC) ---")
for v in m.getVars():
    print(f"{v.VarName}: x={v.X:.0f}, RC={v.RC:.2f}, "
          f"obj range {v.SAObjLow:.0f} to {v.SAObjUp:.0f}")

activities.discussionNote: Shelves carry a negative reduced cost: at a $40 margin they simply cannot outbid desks and chairs for scarce hours. If an AI assistant confidently added shelves to the plan anyway, the RC value is your one-line proof it's wrong. That is the pattern for the AI era — the machine drafts, the sensitivity report testifies, and you deliver the verdict.

takeaways.text: A solved LP is an economic X-ray: shadow prices value every scarce resource, reduced costs explain every excluded option, and ranging tells you exactly when to stop trusting both.
Duality is the deep idea — allocating resources and pricing resources are the same problem viewed from opposite sides, and they always agree at the optimum.
When AI writes the model, sensitivity analysis is your verification layer. An absurd shadow price is the smoke detector for a broken formulation.

homework.label: Homework #2
homework.text: The COO Memo: you are the analytics lead at Meridian Manufacturing. Solve the provided three-product, three-resource LP in gurobipy, then write a one-page memo to your fictional COO answering: (1) which resource to expand first and the maximum price per unit worth paying, (2) whether the discontinued product line deserves a second look and at what margin, (3) how robust the plan is if the top product's price falls 15%. Every claim must cite a specific Pi, RC, or ranging value — but the memo itself must be written in plain executive English with zero jargon. Submit the notebook plus the memo before Session 4.
